newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs to push for swift action on Cuba law.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs to push for swift action on Cuba law.

text.p: The European Parliament plans to step up pressure on the Council to react swiftly to a U.S. law which gives Washington the power to penalise European Union businesses dealing with Cuba.

The parliament's external economic relations committee plans at the assembly's October 21-25 plenary session to ask the Council to say when exactly it intends to react to the extra- territorial provisions of the so-called Helms-Burton Act.
The committee is concerned that the EU is dragging its feet, leaving European firms to face American reprisals without any support.

In its planned oral question to Council, the committee will demand to know when EU ministers will adopt a draft regulation blocking the Act and when they might call for a World Trade Organisation dispute panel to rule on the affair.

A European Commission official told the committee on Wednesday he expected EU foreign ministers provisionally to approve the proposed anti-boycott measures on October 1 and ask parliament urgently to submit its opinion on the text.
Parliament's opinion is needed before the proposed regulation can become law.

He said the Commission was concerned that some member states wished to limit EU-level action to those elements of the Act which contravened EU policy, leaving them to introduce other retaliatory measures through national legislation.
The Commission's did not intend the regulation to provide exclusive powers for the Community but to deal effectively with the problems, he explained.

"It's not only a legal question of covering all these points of Helms-Burton. If the Community wants to have a credible response to American extra-territorial legislation we've got to react quickly and we've got to ensure (the legislation) is applied in all the member states ... in a uniform fashion."

Following a third and final round of consultations with the U.S. on Monday under the aegis of the WTO, the EU could use the next meeting of the WTO dispute settlement body, in mid-October, to request the creation of a panel, a second Commission official told the committee.

The Commission was ready to take that step, he said, and would discuss it with the member states at this week's meeting of the Council's 113 committee on trade matters and at next week's meeting of EU foreign ministers.

He tried to assuage Euro-MPs' fears that the WTO could rule in Washington's favour if the US claimed it needed to apply the Act overseas -- an exception to generally accepted practice -- because U.S. national security was at stake.
By using national security as a defence the U.S. would implicitly be admitting it was in breach of WTO rules under other articles, the official said.
The Commission would need to prepare a response to this eventuality but was confident the EU had a good, if not watertight case and should proceed with a WTO challenge.

As for further retaliatory action, the official said a notice had already been published in the EU's official journal inviting EU firms to supply information on U.S. companies preparing to sue them for alleged trafficking in American property in Cuba seized since the Castro revolution in 1959.
The member states and the Commission were still exploring the possibilitiy of changing EU entry requirements for representatives of U.S. companies, he said.
Under title IV of the Helms-Burton Act, a number of EU executives have been refused entry to the US because they are associated with companies which have investments in Cuba.
